div.p: Feasibility tests for hard real-time systems provide information about the schedulability of a set of tasks. However, this information is a yes or no answer, whether the task set achieves the test or not [13]. From the system design point of view, it would be useful to have more information, for example, how much can vary some task parameters, such as computation time, without jeopardize the system feasibility. The aim of this work is to provide a method to determine how much a task can increase its computation time, maintaining the system feasibility under a dynamic priority scheduling. This extra time can be determined not only in all the task activations, but in n of a window of m task invocations. This is what we call a window-constrained execution time system. This can be very useful in several fields: complex control algorithms, fault tolerance management, imprecise computation, etc. In control applications, this information can be used to execute supervision activities, such as model updating which is not required to be executed all the periods, or to determine new controller parameters for the current operating conditions. In fault tolerance, this information allows to recover n faults in m activations.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Off-line feasibility analysis is fundamental in real-time systems. The scheduler has to meet all deadlines of critical (hard) tasks. In fixed-priority schedulers, feasibility analysis provides information about the task, if any, that miss deadlines. In dynamic priority scheduling algorithms the only information provided by the feasibility test is whether the task set is feasible or not. It would be useful to have more information, for example, how much can vary some task parameters, such as computation time, without jeopardize the system feasibility. Vestal [13] solves the problem of varying task computation times for fixed-priority scheduling. However, no sensitivity analysis has been presented to deal with dynamic priority systems and deadlines different than periods. In this work a method is presented to find the maximum computation time that a task can execute under some temporal constrains, while preserving feasibility. EDF scheduling and deadlines shorter than periods are assumed.

Moreover, this information can be used for industrial control applications, that are usually developed in two phases: control design and real-time system implementation. In the control design stage a regulator is obtained and later it is translated into an algorithm in the implementation phase. Traditionally, these two phases have been developed in separate ways. Recently, some works have pointed out the necessity of the integration of the control design and its implementation [11,5,1,4]. Regarding the integration of real-time control and scheduling, the extra computation time solves two problems: On the one hand, it can be used to switch between more complicated control algorithms that require a greater computation time (Figure 1(a)). On the other hand, in certain situations in practice, a chosen set of controller parameters may not remain valid over the entire range of operating conditions of a plant. The plant dynamics, which is the basis for controller design, may change thereby necessitating redesign and adaptation of the controller. Therefore, the extra time can also be used to update the controller parameters in an adaptive control scheme (Figure 1(b)).

As an example, consider three real-time tasks. Figure 2(a) shows the chronogram of the set executed under EDF scheduling algorithm. As it can be seen, the system is feasible, moreover, the load is not 100%. Let's suppose now that task 1 increases its computation time in 2 units (figure 2(b)). Then, the system is not feasible, since task 3 does not meet We call task 1 scheduled in Figure 2(c) a windowconstrained execution time task, since it executes with an increased computation time not in all the activations, but in n of a window of m invocations. Related work of windowconstrained systems can be found in [3,14]. In these works, a window-constrain system is such a system that guarantees that n deadlines of a window of m activations can be met. In fact, the terminology n m used in this paper is introduced in [3]. However, the meaning is different. In [3] a framework is provided for specifying real-time systems that can tolerate occasional losses of deadlines. However, the purpose of this paper is to provide an schedulability analysis of systems that can increase its computation time following a n m pattern.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In section 2 the terminology is introduced. Section 3 describes the method to obtain the maximum computation time of a task. In section 4 the method is modified to find the computation time increase to execute only in some activations. Section 5 describes the relationships between OCW's. Section 6 shows an example. Finally, in section 7 some conclusions and future lines of work are presented.

div.head: Assumptions and terminology
div.p: For the sake of clarity, consider a set of p periodic tasks τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ p }. Each task τ j = (C j , D j , P j , O j ) is characterized by four parameters: a computation time C j , a period P j , a deadline relative to the release of the task D j , and an offset O j . To consider that a task can vary its computation time some definitions are needed, as well as, introduce a new parameter in the task model: the optional computation window. The following definitions are slightly modified from [3], to take into account the execution time. As an example, consider the same task of the previous example, but now the constrain is 2 4 . Note than now, the n activations are consecutive. Figure 4 presents the chronogram.

Therefore, a task can have a set of pairs {C, n m } that indicates how much can increase its computation time, and how often can do it. This introduces the definition of the optional computation window (OCW):
div.formula: Definition 3 The Optional Computation Window of a task τ j is OCW (j) = {C j + ∆C j , n j m j } Definition 4
div.p: The Optional Computation Window in a row of a task τ j is
div.formula: OCW j = {C j + ∆C j , n j m j }
div.p: For the sake of clarity, from now on, OCW j will be used. Later, we will demonstrate that if the OCW j is feasible, then OCW (j) is feasible too. The OCW j will be introduced as a new parameter in the task model, so now, a task τ C j is defined by five parameters:
div.formula: τ C j = (C j , D j , P j , O j , OCW j ).
div.p: This task is a windowconstrained execution time task.
Furthermore, the following assumptions are made:
• Tasks are periodic.
• C j ≤ D j ≤ P j .
• Tasks are scheduled under EDF scheduling algorithm.
• No resource sharing is considered.
• Only one task (τ C j ) has the OCW parameter. The rest of the tasks are characterized by
div.formula: τ i = (C i , D i , P i , O i ).
div.p: Note that the subscript C refers to a windowconstrained execution time task.

div.head: Exact computation time increase algorithm
div.p: The main goal is to find the ∆C j of task τ C j to meet the restrictions nj mj . This section presents the theory to find the maximum computation time of τ j that can be used in all the activations, or at least that satisfies nj nj 1 . First of all, a review of the existing dynamic scheduling theory is needed.

EDF scheduling algorithm was first described in [9], and it was shown to be optimal in [6]. Unlike fixed-priority scheduling algorithms the first activation of tasks is not the worst, when EDF algorithm is used. [8] showed that the schedulability condition must be checked only in the interval [0, P), being P the hyper-period. In [2] a more accurate feasibility test is proposed, with the same schedulability condition but with a shortest interval to check. In [10] this interval is even more accurate. Moreover, it proposes a new schedulability test based on the idea of Initial Critical Interval (ICI), that is, the first interval [0, R) in which there is no idle time. Other authors refer to this interval as the first busy period. These ideas are summarize in the next theorem:

To increase the computation time of a task, while keeping the other task parameters constant, the only possibility is to use the idle time, that is, when the processor has no remaining computations to serve. This idle time will be used to delay the tasks, and thus, one task of the set will be able to increase its computation time. This way, the idle time is used as a slack time.

div.head: OCW relationships
div.p: Once we know what nj mj satisfies ∆C j , the final step is to compare these values with the initial OCW j of task τ j . The goal is to provide a feasibility test for τ j with OCW j . If the answer is that the task can not meet the deadlines, then, the analysis must provide the correct OCW j that makes the system feasible. Then, the control design stage can have a feedback from the implementation phase that, not only informs wether the task parameters are valid, but provides the correct ones. Therefore, a comparison must be made between the algorithm output OCW i and the initial OCW j . First of all, it is needed the following definition, slightly modified from [3]: Definition 5 Given two temporal constrains OCW 1 and OCW 2 we say that OCW 2 is harder than OCW 1 (and it is denoted by OCW 2 OCW 1 ) when, being OCW 2 feasible then OCW 1 is also feasible.

For example, suppose that OCW 1 = 3 7 and OCW 2 = 3 5 . If OCW 2 is feasible, clearly OCW 1 is also feasible, since OCW 1 is a less demanding constrain than OCW 2 . We can make the window of activations bigger (from 5 to 7), and the 3 activations still can be guaranteed.

If we can assure that OCW i OCW j then τ j will satisfy its constrain, and the system will be feasible. The following theorem, also taken from [3] establishes the general relationship between constrains: Theorem 4 Bernat, 2001 [3]
div.formula: n i m i n j m j ⇐⇒ n j ≤ max{ m j m i n i , m j + m j m i (n i -m i )} Proof: See [3].
div.p: Therefore, if n j does not match the previous expression, or it is bigger, then the task does not meet the constrain and the system is not feasible.

div.p: As an example, consider the task set used in section 1 showed in Table 3. The chronogram of the task set is presented in Figure 2(a)). Applying the algorithm presented in section 3, the maximum computation time that task T1 can execute in all activations is 3 units. The chronogram of the new task set with C 1 = 3 can be seen in Figure 6.

To verify its feasibility, when OCW 1 is applied, it must be executed the algorithm of Table 2 with input ∆C 1 = 4 -2 = 2. The algorithm returns the output values . To know if these constrains are harder than the initial OCW 1 , we apply the last theorem:

Since the calculated n 1 has the same value than the initial one, then the constrain OCW 1 can be satisfied (if 1 4 can be met, then 1 3 can be met too), and the system remains feasible. The chronogram of the task set with task T1 with C 1 = 4 and the constrain 1 3 is showed in Figure 7. Note that for C 1 = 4 the system is not feasible (Figure 2(b)).

div.head: Conclusions and future work
div.p: Feasibility tests allow us to know if a hard real-time system will meet its timing requirements. But no hint is provided to the designers to make the system feasible. It would be very interesting to know what would happen if we vary task parameters, such as computation times.

This paper has dealt with the problem of knowing how much can the parameter C j increase without making the system unfeasible, for dynamic-priority algorithms. The method has been proved to be exact, that is, we obtain the maximum computation time for a task, while the other task parameters are invariant. Moreover, a new task parameter has been defined, the Optional Computation Window (OCW) that indicates the number of activations within a window that a task can execute with a greater computation time. This allows a task to execute more complex algorithms, improving the control performance of the system, or to redesign the controller, in an adaptive control scheme. Moreover, if the OCW is not valid, we can provide the valid one, that can be used as a feedback by the control designers to redefine the control system.

Further research is concerned with combining OCW of more than one task. Experimental measures are needed to know how the control action is improved by executing more complex algorithms. This way, the real-time system will be flexible enough to adapt to the dynamic system requirements.
